items: The records of the kings of the Hatti, the great empire of the east, name a city on the western sea: WILUSA — the city the Greeks call Troy. Its king was bound to the Great King of the Hatti by treaty and oath.

And the same records name sea-raiders out of the west, from the land the Hatti called AHHIYAWA — the land of the Achaeans. Between the empire and the sea stood Wilusa. So much the clay remembers. The rest is the singer's.
*HATTI — the great empire of inner Anatolia, east of Troy; its ruler was called the Great King.
On the third evening there was no room left on the benches of Miletus.
The mountain, father. The apple. You promised.

And you shall have them, child. But the apple falls on a mountain above Troy — so first you must see Troy as it was in those days: rich, pious, and caught between the hammer of the east and the sea-wolves of the west.
Muse, sing through me: sing of Wilusa between the empires — of a queen's terrible dream, of a child left on a mountain, and of a wedding in heaven's sight where Strife came uninvited.
Hear then, as the Muse gives it.
This is Troy in the days of its greatness — a lifetime after Heracles broke its wall, a lifetime before the ships came.
Priam the purchased had grown into the richest king of the west of Asia — just, pious, and blessed in children.
His queen was Hecuba, mother of princes. Their eldest son was Hector — you will hear that name until you are weary of glory. Their house seemed built past all shaking.
The city is at peace, my lord. The gods are kind.
The gods are owed, wife. My father learned it. Peace is a wage we pay for daily.
Twice a year the tablets came from the east — from the Great King of the Hatti, to whom Troy was bound by old treaty and oath.
"...thus speaks the Great King: keep my roads, keep my peace on the shore, and my protection stands over Wilusa as the sky stands over the earth."
The oath binds both ways, my king. We keep the Great King's peace; he keeps the spear of the east from our backs. It is a good bargain — while both sides keep it.
And the west, Antenor? Who binds the sea? Ahhiyawan keels were seen off the islands again this spring — the raiders ask no one's leave!
Troy has stood between hammer and water since my grandfather's day. Hear the whole of it, and learn how a city lives.

To the east — faith. We keep our oath to the Hatti to the last written word, and their strength shadows us. To the west — watchfulness and open harbors. A raider who can trade would rather trade. We fortify the shore, we tax the strait, we feast the stranger who comes in peace.

So Troy balanced, year upon year, and grew rich on the balance. It was wisely done. Remember, princes, that it was wisely done — for what broke Troy in the end was none of the things its wise men guarded against.

In the tenth year of that peace, Hecuba the queen, carrying a child, dreamed a dream: she gave birth not to a child but to a burning torch — and the fire of it took hold of Troy, and the whole city burned to the waterline.
The dream was told to the seers, and the lots were cast, and the answer came back with one voice.
The child the queen carries will be the burning of Troy. If Troy would live... the child must not.
What the seers asked, no father's heart could do and no king's heart could refuse. Priam chose as a king — and paid as a father, every day after.
Take him to the high mountain, Agelaus. Do not tell me where. Do not tell me anything, ever.

Agelaus was a kind man given a cruel task. He carried the child five days into the wilds of Ida — and found he could not use the knife. He laid the boy in a sheltered hollow, and fled, and wept as he went.
And the gods, who had their own use for that child, sent a she-bear. Five days she suckled him as her own.
Alive... Then the gods refuse the seers' price. Come, little one. What heaven keeps, no man may spill. You are my son now — and no one's else.

The boy grew on the mountain, knowing nothing of Troy, of dreams, of seers. The herdsmen called him Alexandros — "defender of men" — for he beat the raiders from their herds while still half a boy. He was the fairest thing on that mountain, and the mountain knew it.
Agelaus raised him as his own and told him nothing. But some nights the old man looked at the boy's face — a face too fine for any herdsman's son — and was afraid of what he had saved.
And sometimes the boy looked down at the shining city on the plain and felt a thing he had no name for. Blood knows its house, princes, even when the house has barred the door.
At the herdsmen's autumn contest, Alexandros's own bull — his pride, his hand-raised champion — stood against a white bull that no man on Ida had ever seen before.
And the white bull won. It was not close.
The garland is yours, stranger's bull. My heart wanted otherwise — but the garland is yours.

He crowned the stranger's bull over his own. Mark that little judgment on a mountain, princes — heaven was watching it. Fairness in a small thing is how the gods choose men for great ones. It is also how they choose their instruments.
The abandoned child judges fairly on the mountain... while his father judges tablets in the city below. And neither knows the other lives.

You begin to hear how the song is built, child. Now hold Troy and the mountain in your mind — and come west with me, across the sea and up another mountain. For while the boy grew on Ida, the gods were preparing a wedding.
And with that wedding, the last piece of the plan of Zeus was set moving.
In the sea lived Thetis — a goddess, kindest of the daughters of the old sea-god. Zeus himself had desired her. Poseidon had desired her.
Hear the decree that stands over her, lord of gods: THE SON OF THETIS WILL BE GREATER THAN HIS FATHER. Take her, and you raise your own overthrow.

Then no god may wed her. Let her be given to a mortal man — the worthiest alive. Her son will be the greatest of mortals... and mortal. So the decree is satisfied — and so is my plan. For I will need that son.
Remember this, princes: the greatest of all heroes will be born not from love, but from heaven's caution.

The worthiest mortal alive was Peleus, king of Phthia — not the strongest, not the richest: the most god-fearing. Heaven's choice fell on him, and he was told what he must do to win a goddess: find her on the shore, take hold of her, and not let go.
She became water in his arms, and he held. Fire, and he held. Lioness and serpent, and he held. All night he held what no man should be able to hold.
You held, mortal. And having won me... you kneel?
A man may hold a goddess, lady. He should not therefore forget what he is holding.
And it was the kneeling, not the holding, that won her.
Understand what you take, Peleus. I am deathless. You will age and die. And our son — our son I will love as goddesses love: helplessly, and without power to keep him.
She consented, and heaven rejoiced, and she grieved. Hold her grief in mind, princes. It runs beneath the whole rest of this song like a river under a battlefield.
The wedding was set on Mount Pelion, at the cave of Chiron — the wise centaur*, teacher of heroes, gentlest of all the immortal-blooded.
*CENTAUR — a being half man and half horse. Most were wild; Chiron alone was wise and kind, and princes were sent to him to be taught.
Every god and goddess of heaven was invited by name — the herald of the gods carried the summons himself.

Every god and goddess — except one. Eris, the goddess of Strife, was not summoned. For who invites Strife to a wedding? Learn the answer of this song, princes: Strife needs no invitation. She only needs a door.
And heaven emptied onto the mountain. Never before and never after did all the gods sit as guests at a mortal man's marriage.
And one mortal man stood to receive them, and did not disgrace himself.
The bride was led in veiled in silver. The gods saw her beauty. Only her sisters of the sea saw her eyes.

So Peleus wed Thetis on Pelion, with heaven itself for wedding-guests, and the Muses sang the marriage-song. Men told of that night for a hundred generations: the last feast at which gods and mortals rejoiced together at one table.
Cut from the ash of this mountain, friend, for the son you will have. I have shaped it heavy. He will not find it so.
Remember the ash spear of Pelion, princes. In all the years of the great war to come, only one man will ever be able to lift it.
And Poseidon gave two deathless horses, Balius and Xanthus, swift as the west wind that sired them. Remember the horses too. A day is coming when one of them will be given a voice — and will weep.

Every gift on that table was for the son to come. And the bride smiled, and thanked the givers, and heard under all the music the one truth she could not drown: the gifts of gods are given to mortals because mortals die.
And at the height of the joy, Strife came to the edge of the light.
She carried one gift of her own: an apple of solid gold. And on it one thing was written — "FOR THE FAIREST."
A wedding-gift... for whichever of you is fairest. Heaven may decide.
She asked for no seat and no cup. She needed neither. Strife's whole feast is in the throwing.
She threw it into the middle of the feast — and was gone before it landed.
It came to rest — the singer does not think by chance — exactly between three thrones.
The song stopped. And the last feast of gods and mortals ended — not with a quarrel of men, but with a quarrel of heaven.
I am the queen of heaven and the wife of its king. The word on this gold names me.
Wisdom is the highest beauty, and victory the fairest of all things. The word names me.
Sisters. Read the word again — and look at me. The word names me.
Three goddesses; one word; no shared measure of "fairest." Princes, when a quarrel has no shared measure, it has no peaceful end. Remember this hour when the ships burn.
Not I. Whichever of you I crowned, I would set two immortal angers at my own table forever. This gold needs a judge with nothing to lose that a god would fear to lose.
There is a herdsman on Ida, above Troy. He once crowned a stranger's bull over his own champion, because it was fair. Let the fairest be judged... by the fairest judge among mortals.
So spoke Zeus. And if you ask whether he knew whose son that herdsman was, and what would follow — ask rather whether the plan of Zeus was ever, for one hour of this song, not walking.
Hermes the herald was given the apple and the charge: bring the three goddesses to the herdsman of Ida.
And the four went east through the night, over the sea, the apple carried like a lamp before them.
Toward one small fire on a mountainside — and the most dangerous question ever put to a mortal man.
In Troy that night, no one looked at the mountain. Priam's house was full: Hector the eldest, already the best of the young men of Asia; and children beyond counting.
And one daughter, Cassandra — to whom Apollo had given true sight of what is to come; and because she slighted the god, this also: that no one would ever believe her.
*Her gift and her curse in full is a tale for a later night; what matters now is this — she alone, of all Troy, felt the light on the mountain.
Mother... there are torches on Ida. Walking torches. Tell them to put out the torches on Ida...
No one heard her. No one ever would.
"...thus speaks the Great King: it is heard that the western sea is quiet this year. Keep it so, and the gods of the oath keep Wilusa."
Quiet to the east, quiet to the west. I have served three kings, my lord, and never known the city safer.
Then we are watchful in all four directions, old friend.

In all four directions. But doom was not coming from any of the four directions. It was already inside the walls of the world — on their own mountain, in their own blood, wearing a herdsman's kilt. No treaty in any archive had a clause for that.
Count it with me, lord of gods. The Earth's plea — heard. The instrument of beauty — born, and wed to Sparta. The kings of Greece — bound by their own oath.

The greatest of heroes — begotten this very season of Peleus and Thetis. Troy — rich, faithful, and owing. And now three goddesses and one golden question... walking up the mountain to the hidden prince.

The board is set, the pieces placed, and every piece was moved by its own will — the seers chose, the father chose, the herdsman will choose. When it is done, no man and no god will be able to say the choice was not theirs. That is the whole art of my plan, Themis. It has no hands. It needs none.
And on the mountain, the herdsman played to his cattle in the evening light, and knew nothing at all.
He did not know his name was a king's son's name. He did not know a burning torch had been dreamed of him. He did not know that heaven was on his path.
He was, at that hour, the freest and happiest man in this whole long song. Look at him well, princes. The next time the Muse shows him to us, he will be choosing for all mankind.
And the herdsman does not know, father. The king does not know. Only the mad girl knows — and no one hears her.

Now you have the shape of it, child. That is how doom walks in the songs and in the world: not through the gates the watchmen watch, but up the path no one thought to guard — and always, always announced by one voice that no one believes.
Ask yourself, prince of Miletus — you who will rule men: which voice in your own hall is the one you are not believing?
Enough. The child is grown, the wedding is sung, the apple is thrown, and three goddesses stand on the mountain path.
Tomorrow, the judgment — three goddesses, three bribes, and a herdsman's choice. And after it, child... after it, a ship sails for Sparta.
"Delusion is the elder daughter of Zeus. Her feet are soft, for she does not walk upon the ground — she walks upon the heads of men."
— after words spoken in the song of the wrath, when a king confessed his blindness.
